name: Dark Hot Pink
lede: Dark Hot Pink is a deep magenta-pink recorded on Robert Ridgway's 1912 color plates decades before the 2010 xkcd survey gave it this exact modern name, and the two sources' hues sit close together.

sections.title: A 1912 plate and a 2010 name
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912) plates a closely matching hue on plate XII, hue 69 [5]. The color library separately dates the first recorded use of a near-identical name to 1905, via Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, which cites earlier sources [2]. Nearly a century later, the xkcd survey of 2010 recorded *dark hot pink* as a modifier built on the existing name [[hot-pink]], from thousands of volunteers naming swatches on screen [1].

Ridgway's plate is a scan of an aged printed page, so its color is approximate, while the xkcd hex value, #D90166, comes from a monitor swatch; the two measuring methods should not be expected to match exactly [2][5]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system separately places the hue in its vivid purplish red block, 5.4 units off [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[rubine-red]], [[razzmatazz]] and [[red-purple]], at 3.7, 3.9 and 4 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our 23,781-painting archive, a color within six units of Dark Hot Pink covers at least one per cent of the canvas in just 1 painting, as photographed, rarer than 86 percent of the named colors tracked [3]. A pink this saturated and dark is hard for most historical pigments to reach; where it does appear, it is more likely a trick of varnish and lighting than a deliberate match to either Ridgway's plate or the modern crayon-box pink [3]. The Ngram data does not find a clean peak for the exact phrase, which stays rare throughout the record [4].
